sources.news_title: Beloved SoCal Bald Eagle Dies, Sending Fans Worldwide Into Mourning
sources.text:
Community Corner
Beloved SoCal Bald Eagle Dies, Sending Fans Worldwide Into Mourning
Despite receiving round-the-clock monitoring, her condition progressively deteriorated over the past several days.
OJAI, CA — Jackie, a critically ill Big Bear bald eagle that drew global support during weeks of intensive medical care at Ojai Raptor Center, has died, the facility announced Monday afternoon.
The eagle, identified as Patient 26-519 by Ojai Raptor Center, passed away early Monday morning after more than three weeks of treatment, according to the facility.
Despite receiving round-the-clock monitoring, oxygen therapy, and supportive care in the center's intensive care unit, the bird's condition progressively deteriorated over the past several days, according to veterinary staff and consulting specialists.
Find out what's happening in Banning-Beaumontfor free with the latest updates from Patch.
The eagle's remains have been transferred to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
Center officials expressed deep gratitude to the thousands of supporters worldwide who followed the eagle's recovery effort, noting that staff are working closely with federal and state wildlife agencies to release a comprehensive report detailing the bird's treatment and medical test results.
Find out what's happening in Banning-Beaumontfor free with the latest updates from Patch.
"To everyone who cared about Patient 26-519, thank you. Thank you for your messages, your prayers, your encouragement, and for standing beside our team throughout these past weeks," the center shared on social media. "We are deeply grateful for the way Patient 26-519 brought people together through a shared love of wildlife."
Friends of Big Bear Valley and Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam posted a short, poignant message to social media: "Soar free Jackie…"
The news brought an outpouring a sadness from Jackie supporters.
"Her purpose was great and she served it with profound strength," one person shared on social media. "She helped replenish the Bald Eagle population, brought thousands of people together, gave us hope and enjoyment. Most of all her life helped to save Big Bear. She used her time here well without even knowing it. She is loved and now its time for her to eternally be at rest and in peace."
Another wrote, "I hope her death can help the veterinary teams deal with future issues when they occur to these beautiful birds. Fly high Jackie."
Jackie was rescued nearly a month ago after being found grounded and unable to fly near Big Bear Lake’s Dana Point Park. Members of the Los Angeles County San Dimas Raptor Rescue Team retrieved the approximately 14-year-old raptor before transferring her to the Ojai facility.
The bird's medical journey saw sharp fluctuations. After receiving a life-saving blood transfusion from a donor eagle, she showed signs of improvement and was moved out of the intensive care unit, where she had been receiving oxygen therapy, into a regular hospital care unit. Though her blood values temporarily stabilized, the root cause of her severe anemia remains unidentified despite extensive testing, which previously ruled out lead toxicosis and swallowed fishing tackle.
Jackie’s nest life above Big Bear Lake alongside her mate, Shadow, was watched by millions worldwide via a 24/7 livestream "Nest Cam" hosted by Friends of Big Bear Valley. Her global popularity recently inspired a major conservation victory when donors — including OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna — contributed $5.5 million to purchase and protect the surrounding habitat around the nest from real estate development.
The bald eagle couple successfully raised two eaglets, Luna and Sandy, earlier this year. Both fledged in late June and are believed to be thriving in the wild.

sources.news_title: Social media-famous bald eagle Jackie dies after weeks of intensive medical care
sources.text:
Big Bear bald eagle Jackie, made famous by a 24/7 webcast operated by the environmental nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley, died in the early morning hours of Aug. 10.
She died away from her nest and apart from her eaglets and mate. But the beloved bird of prey was never alone.
People from across several continents tuned in to the livestream by phone or television, elevating the raptor to celebrity status and weaving the happenings at a nest atop a pine tree into the daily ritual of people’s lives. For nearly a month, a congregation of virtual bird watchers shifted their attention from the nest to a Ventura-based wildlife center that was caring for Jackie after she was found grounded in mid-July following a fight with two other young adult eagles.
Ojai Raptor Center, the rescue and rehab site administering medical care for Jackie, updated its Facebook page on Monday, Aug. 10, saying the cherished raptor had “passed away.” A cause of death was not given.
“Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists. She remained critically ill, receiving oxygen therapy, supportive treatment, and around-the-clock monitoring in our intensive care unit,” the Ojai post reads.
Jackie’s remains have been transferred into the care of the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, according to the Ojai facility.
“We are working closely with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results,” the Ojai post says.
The Friends group confirmed the news on their social media channels.
“It is with great sadness and heavy hearts to bring you the latest update from Ojai Raptor Center. Please be kind to yourself, to others, to the FOBBV team and to those at the Ojai Raptor Center. Soar free, Jackie,” the Friends post reads.
Jackie’s medical care yielded promising uptrends and troubling downturns.
Weeks earlier, Jackie underwent a successful, late-night blood transfusion. The wildlife center called the procedure “life-saving.”
On Sunday, Aug. 9, Ojai update reported that Jackie remained “critically ill,” with low levels of packed cell volume — the percentage of red blood cells in the bloodstream.
Jackie’s fanbase stretches across the globe. Since the first installation in October 2015 and a second in 2021, Friends of Big Bear Valley’s social media has exploded, with approximately 2.4 million followers, including over 1 million on its main Facebook page and close to 400,000 in a private Facebook group. It’s typical that each social media post shared by FBBV rakes in thousands of comments, likes and shares.
The late Friends executive director, Sandy Steers, said that broadcasting the daily lives of bald eagles was part of the nonprofit’s vision to raise environmental awareness.
“Protecting and conserving Jackie and Shadow’s unique and irreplaceable habitat through monitoring, education and advocacy and also helping humans connect with nature,” Steers said by email in January.
And for over 10 years, the nest has garnered millions of eyes.
Jackie was born in 2012 to Ricky and Lucy, two Big Bear eagles named by the U.S. National Forest Service. She fledged from the nest that summer. When Friends group installed its first livestream camera, the nest was empty. In fall 2016, an adult female began visiting the nesting site with the camera. The group concluded she was roughly Jackie’s age and had feather patterns similar to Jackie’s before fledging in 2012.
“We believe she stayed in Big Bear,” Friends of Big Bear Valley stated on its website. Jackie later moved into the nest, mated with a previous partner, “Mr. B,” and raised eaglets in 2018. Shadow arrived later that year, and Mr. B left the area.
Since then, Jackie and Shadow have continued to lay eggs and raise eaglets.
This year’s 2026 eaglets, Sandy and Luna, have flown from the nest and were last seen on July 23, Friends reports.
For nearly a month, an extended eagle family from across the globe held their breath. Many hoped for a reunion with her lifelong mate, Shadow.
Now a community says goodbye.
“It was wonderful to have the opportunity of following both Jackie and Shadow, such beautiful eagles. Nature has a way of letting go. Fly high above the Big Bear area, Jackie; you will always be remembered,” Ros Willis commented on the Friends of Big Bear Valley Monday post.
Another comment made by Jen Coolidge said, “Jackie, you are and forever will be one of the biggest Wildlife stories ever told. Thank you for allowing us all to love you, your family and be a part of your journey through nest cameras.”
This story is developing. Please check back later for more Jackie coverage.

sources.news_title: Celebrity bald eagle Jackie has died after weeks of deteriorating health
sources.text:
Celebrity bald eagle Jackie has died after weeks of deteriorating health
Jackie the bald eagle, who became famous for raising several eaglets in Big Bear, California, with her partner Shadow, has died following weeks of deteriorating health.
The eagle pair became internet favorites thanks to a live nest camera operated by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley, which allows people around the world to watch their daily lives.
Jackie had been nesting in the Big Bear area for years, where she and Shadow have raised eaglets together. Their nest sat high in a Jeffrey pine tree near Big Bear Lake, more than 7,000 feet above sea level.
Jackie became especially popular for her dedicated parenting, dramatic interactions with Shadow and the challenges she faced protecting eggs and chicks from harsh mountain weather.
But weeks ago, Jackie entered intensive medical care when she was found weak and unable to fly.
She was taken to Ojai Raptor Center for specialized care, where veterinarians discovered that she was suffering from severe anemia and kidney inflammation.
Her condition had significant ups and downs over the last few weeks. But officials with the organization announced Monday that Jackie had died.
"Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists," a statement from the facility reads in part. "She remained critically ill, receiving oxygen therapy, supportive treatment, and around-the-clock monitoring in our intensive care unit."
Her remains have been transferred into the care of the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
"We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her," officials with the Ojai Raptor Center said. "Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her."

sources.news_title: Jackie the bald eagle dead at 14
sources.text:
Jackie, a bald eagle with a devoted internet following, died early in the morning on August 10 in Ojai, California, while in the care of the Ojai Raptor Center. She was 14 years old.
The Ojai Raptor Center announced her death and it was shared by Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the nonprofit who monitors the eagles of Big Bear Valley.
“Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists,” the center writes. “She remained critically ill, receiving oxygen therapy, supportive treatment, and around-the-clock monitoring in our intensive care unit. Throughout her time at Ojai Raptor Center, every decision was guided by the available medical evidence, her welfare, and our responsibility to do what was in her best interest.”
Jackie’s remains have been transferred into the care of the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).
“Soar free Jackie,” FOBBV wrote on Facebook.
Jackie’s story
Jackie was born, raised, and lived in Big Bear Valley in southern California. Prior to the 2011-2012 nesting season, no bald eagle chicks were known to have ever hatched in Big Bear Valley. Then came Jackie, named after a forest ranger and born to parents Ricky and Lucy in 2012.
During the 2016-2017 nesting season, Jackie took over a nest where Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV) had a camera stationed. In 2018, she had two chicks named Stormy and Big Bear Baby (or BBB) with her first mate, Mr. B.
Her long-time partner Shadow entered the picture in summer 2018. He showed up at the nest and would not leave. FOBBV called the new male Shadow because he appeared so determined to stay in the nest, and the team initially believed he was one of Jackie’s siblings, also named Shadow. The eagle’s plumage indicated he was one year older than the other Shadow and not Jackie’s sibling, but the name stuck.
Shadow continued to hold his ground and Mr. B gave up and eventually left. Jackie then accepted Shadow as her new mate.
Wildlife cameras documented Jackie and Shadow’s life together, offering viewers a direct look into the brutality and beauty of nature. The pair successfully raised chicks in 2019 (Cookie and Simba) and 2022 (Spirit). The pair’s eggs failed to hatch in 2023 and 2024. In 2025, Jackie laid three eggs that all hatched in early March. However, a strong snowstorm dumped up to two feet of snow and battered the nest with strong wind and only two of the chicks (Sunny and Gizmo) survived.
In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and were later named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.
Jackie’s injury
On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.
She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below six percent, before rising to nine percent.
Jackie’s resilience inspired millions of people around the world.
To honor Jackie’s memory, FOBBV accepts donations to support its conservation efforts in the area. You can help the rescue organization nursing Jackie back to health by donating to Ojai Raptor Center’s Bald Eagle Recovery Campaign.
Cards can be mailed to:
Ojai Raptor Center
Attn: Patient 26-519
P.O. Box 182
Oak View, CA 93022
This is a developing story and we will continue to share updates from The Ojai Raptor Center and Friends of Big Bear Valley as they become available.

sources.news_title: Jackie, the Big Bear bald eagle, dies in Southern California
sources.text:
Jackie, the Big Bear bald eagle, dies in Southern California
Jackie the bald eagle has died.
The Ojai Raptor Center said the famous eagle died on Monday morning following three weeks of medical care.
“Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists. She remained critically ill, receiving oxygen therapy, supportive treatment, and around-the-clock monitoring in our intensive care unit,” the Ojai Raptor Center said in a statement.
The group said its team was “heartbroken” by the development.
Jackie had been rescued and underwent rehabilitation at the center after a fight with other eagles. Her condition worsened, though, and the raptor center said she was anemic.
Millions have come to know Jackie and her partner Shadow by watching livestreams from the Friends of Big Bear Valley’s nest cams. Learn more about the eagle's history here.
The Friends of Big Bear Valley said on Facebook that the update of Jackie's passing brought "great sadness and heavy hearts."
"Please be kind to yourself, to others, to the FOBBV team and to those at the Ojai Raptor Center," the group wrote. "Soar free Jackie."

sources.news_title: Jackie, arguably the world's most famous bald eagle, dies after weeks of treatment
sources.text:
Jackie, arguably the world’s most famous bald eagle, dies after mysterious illness
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
After a weeks-long battle with a mysterious illness, Big Bear’s beloved bald eagle Jackie died Monday morning at an Ojai rehabilitation center. She was 14.
Jackie and her mate, Shadow, delighted millions of viewers as stars of a nonstop livestream of their nest, perched high in a Jeffrey pine overlooking Big Bear Lake. Since the pair formed in 2018, fans have watched them weather freezing winter storms, incubate eggs and dote on fuzzy chicks.
But in mid-July, Jackie was found weak, disheveled and unable to fly on the north shore of the lake following a scuffle with two younger eagles. She was rescued and transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center, where experts treated her until her death.
“We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her and supported the people caring for her,” the center wrote in an Instagram post.
Big Bear eagle Jackie has passed. We want to hear fans’ favorite memories of her and her family.
“Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her.”
In an earlier post, Chris Eksteen, the center’s executive director, said fighting likely left Jackie grounded but did not cause her symptoms. Tests revealed she had severe anemia, leading to a blood transfusion from another eagle.
“What we are seeing suggests that she has been unwell for some time before she was found,” he said in an Instagram post this month.
Despite a battery of tests, including a contrast CT scan and bone marrow biopsy, experts could not determine what was making Jackie critically ill.
Since arriving in Ojai, her health journey was uneven. Her blood values, including packed cell volume — which measures the percentage of red blood cells in the bloodstream — increased and fell several times.
About a week and a half into her care, she was moved out of the intensive care unit, offering a glimmer of hope. But on Aug. 3, the center reported her packed cell volume fell to 13%, meaning her anemia had worsened. On Saturday, it dipped below 6% before rebounding to 9% the following day.
“Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists,” the Ojai center said in its announcement.
She was receiving oxygen therapy, supportive treatment and nonstop monitoring in the ICU, the center said.
Jackie’s remains have been transferred to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. The center said it is working with that department and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and will provide another statement with more information about her treatment and test results.
News of Jackie’s death sent ripples of mourning through her fan base. Thousands took to social media to express their condolences and praise the avian matriarch.
“She lived an incredible life and inspired many,” Facebook user Jordan Markowski wrote. “Who knows how many people have and will go on to do great things to preserve and protect wild spaces and creatures because of her.
“And now in her final act, albeit unknowingly, she’s made space for the next generation of eagles in the circle of life.”
“I’ll never forget this period of knowing Jackie and Shadow. They have been such a light in the dark times that we are having in the US,” Margie Boyd Stansell wrote on Facebook.
Jackie’s rise to reality stardom began after Friends of Big Bear Valley installed a webcam in 2015 to capture the goings-on of her parents’ nest. Unbeknownst to the nonprofit, that couple — dubbed Ricky and Lucy — had shifted to a new nest and soon left the area altogether.
An eagle believed to be Jackie started hanging around the old nest. A male, called Mr. B., joined her.
During the summer of 2018, “an adult male intruder showed up to the nest and, with great tenacity, refused to leave,” Friends of Big Bear Valley wrote. Mr. B. eventually moved on, and the interloper, dubbed Shadow, moved in.
In 2021, a second camera was added to capture a wider view of the eagles’ habitat.
In their eight years nesting together, Jackie and Shadow raised numerous chicks and bonded as they restored their nest.
But raw, unadulterated nature delivers both sorrow and joy. In late January, the couple’s clutch of two eggs was eaten by ravens. Not long after, Sandy Steers, executive director of Friends of Big Bear Valley, died after a private battle with cancer.
Jackie laid another pair of eggs in late February. That clutch was successful, with the two eaglets — Luna and Sandy — fledging this summer.
Sandy, named to honor Steers, and brother Luna were last seen on camera on July 23. “It appears they have left the valley on their grand journey,” the nonprofit wrote on Facebook.
Colleagues of Steers carried on her mission, including an effort to raise $10 million to buy land near the eagles’ nest that was slated for development. In late July, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, donated $5.5 million to the cause. That large infusion, along with thousands of smaller donations, surpassed the fundraising goal. A land trust now will steward the roughly 63 acres.
Since Jackie’s rescue, fans have wondered what will become of Shadow and the life she left behind in Big Bear.
Friends of Big Bear Valley acknowledged it’s impossible to know what the future holds. Shadow, who is 12, could find a new mate or even leave the Big Bear area.

sources.news_title: Beloved bald eagle Jackie dies after health battle and 'critical' illness
sources.text:
Beloved bald eagle Jackie dies after health battle and 'critical' illness
Beloved bald eagle Jackie died while rehabilitating at a wildlife center in California after being rescued following an apparent "altercation" with two subadult eagles.
"It is with profound sadness that we share that Patient 26-519 passed away in the early hours of this morning, following more than three weeks of intensive medical care," Ojai Raptor Center, where Jackie has been receiving treatment for almost a month, said in an Aug. 10 update. "Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her."
In the same update, the Ojai Raptor Center said that Jackie's remains had been transferred into the care of the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
The beloved bald eagle known for appearing on Big Bear Valley's Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam was "critically ill" and unstable before she died, the center had said in its last update on Aug. 9.
Friends of Big Bear Valley's Big Bear Eagle Nest Cam (FOBBV), which manages the eagle nest cam, mourned Jackie's loss in a post on Facebook, telling the eagle's fans to be "kind to yourself, to others, to the FOBBV team and to those at the Ojai Raptor Center."
"Soar free Jackie," the center said.
What happened to Big Bear's Jackie?
It all started after Jackie was seen in an "altercation" with two subadult eagles on July 17. While Jackie was able to defend herself, she did not get far and was seen on the ground near Dana Point Park, where she was rescued and taken to Ojai Raptor Center, about 170 miles from her home in California's Big Bear Valley, which she shares with her long-term partner Shadow.
"Initial bloodwork" had indicated Jackie was "experiencing severe anemia and inflammation affecting the kidneys," the center said on July 21. Vets had begun "supportive treatment based on the information available," with guidance from wildlife professionals globally.
Over the next few weeks, Jackie would undergo rigorous testing and treatment as vets worked round-the-clock to diagnose her illness.
Ojai Raptor Center, in its last update on Jackie's health, said Jackie's packed cell volume had fallen below 6% on Aug. 8 but rose to 9% on Aug. 9.
"The past 24 hours have been incredibly difficult," the center had said, adding that her condition remains "extremely serious."
"Her care and condition are being closely evaluated by a collaborative team that includes nine veterinarians, together with representatives from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife," the center said.
Jackie received 'life-saving' blood transfusion
Earlier, despite showing small but encouraging signs of recovery, Jackie's anemia had worsened, with her latest bloodwork bringing "difficult news," Ojai Raptor Center said on Aug. 3. Jackie's packed cell volume had dropped to 13%, which meant her anemia had worsened.
The facility said its "veterinary team is responding quickly," and "additional advanced diagnostic testing" is underway as it continues "working to better understand her condition and guide the next steps in her treatment."
Jackie, on July 20, also received a "life-saving" blood transfusion from another eagle and underwent oxygen therapy as part of her treatment. She was also treated for rodenticide toxicity, which occurs when humans or nontarget animals ingest rat or mouse poisons, although caregivers do not believe that is the primary cause of her illness.
Several other possible causes, such as lead poisoning, cancer and metal objects, were ruled out through extensive testing. On July 23, wildlife agencies had said test results show Jackie does not have lead poisoning, a common killer among bald eagles and other birds.
A star is born
Jackie was the first eaglet to be hatched in Big Bear Valley in 2012, USA TODAY previously reported. Her parents, Ricky and Lucy, became the first known adult eagles who decided to stay in Big Bear Valley, which until then had only been a part-time winter destination for the species.
Big Bear resident Sandy Steers, who was also the executive director of Friends of Big Bear Valley, lived half a mile from where Jackie was born and watched her grow up from a distance. It was Steers, and a U.S. Forest Service employee, who got the idea to put up a webcam. It took two years to raise the $10,000 needed to buy and install the solar-powered camera, which sits 120 feet off the forest floor.
Jackie lived in relative eagle obscurity before the webcam was installed.
"You could see her practicing flying, you could see them [Lucy and Ricky] bringing her food," Steers had told USA TODAY. "I stood there for hours every day just watching because I was fascinated. That got me hooked and then I just wanted to see more."
Steers described Jackie as "very determined, very serious, and she expects to get her way."
Jackie found her first romance in 2017 when she mated with an eagle named Mr. B. The couple's eggs hatched in 2018, and while one of the eaglets died after a 24-hour rainstorm, the other, named Stormy, survived and left Big Bear that summer.
However, Mr. B and Jackie's romance did not last long and soon after Shadow swooped in, chased off Mr. B and stole Jackie's heart. The two have been together ever since.
What is Jackie's family up to?
Friends of Big Bear Valley, which manages the popular nest cam, said Jackie's ill health marks a "season of uncertainty" for the beloved eagle family.
"This season certainly has had its ups and downs, sad times and good times," FOBBV said Aug. 5. Even so, Jackie, Shadow, Sandy and Luna brought us immense amounts of Joy.
As Jackie received treatment, her eaglets, Sandy and Luna, appeared to have taken off for the wild. They were last seen on the cam on July 23.
Jackie's partner, Shadow, meanwhile, is on "his summer vacation," FOBBV said. "He has been and will likely continue to be seen on camera occasionally."
However, millions of fans are worried about the power couple's fate after a new young female, believed to have attacked Jackie before her hospitalization, was seen perched with Shadow.
Many on social media have taken to calling the new eagle Jolene after the famed female rival from the Dolly Parton song of the same name. Though wildlife professionals and others take umbrage with the nickname, they can't deny her interest in Shadow.
"She's obviously gravitating towards him," said Jenny Voisard, a spokeswoman for Friends of Big Bear Valley, the group that runs the live nest camera that made Jackie and Shadow famous. "Maybe something deep inside her says, 'I want to be by this eagle. He's pretty awesome.'"
Experts, however, believe Shadow isn't likely to be ready to move on from his life with Jackie. The pair have been together for nearly a decade and have shared eight eaglets.
This story was updated with more information.
Contributing: Michelle Del Rey, Anthony Thompson, Amanda Lee Myers, Julia Gomez
Saman Shafiq is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach her at sshafiq@usatodayco.com and follow her on X and Instagram @saman_shafiq7.

sources.news_title: Jackie, beloved Big Bear bald eagle watched by millions, dies
sources.text:
Jackie, beloved Big Bear bald eagle watched by millions, dies
For nearly a decade, millions of people around the world watched mama Jackie battle snowstorms, raise eaglets and help turn a remote nest overlooking Big Bear Lake into one of California's most beloved wildlife attractions.
Jackie, the celebrity bald eagle whose life was followed by a global audience through the Friends of Big Bear Valley livestream cameras, died at age 14 after undergoing treatment for a serious illness. The Ojai Raptor Center announced that she died "in the early hours of this morning" in an update shared on social media in the afternoon of Monday, Aug. 10.
"Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists," the Ojai Raptor Center said. "She remained critically ill, receiving oxygen therapy, supportive treatment, and around-the-clock monitoring in our intensive care unit."
Her death marks the end of an extraordinary chapter in California wildlife conservation and closes a story that transformed a bald eagle into an unlikely internet star.
"We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her," the Ojai Raptor Center said. "Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her."
The Ojai Raptor Center said Jackie's remains have been transferred into the care of the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
The Friends of Big Bear Valley shared the news from the Ojai Raptor Center on their Facebook page with a brief caption.
"It is with great sadness and heavy hearts, to bring you the latest update from Ojai Raptor Center," the Friends of Big Bear Valley said. "Please be kind to yourself, to others, to the FOBBV team and to those at the Ojai Raptor Center. Soar free Jackie…"
The eagle who put Big Bear on screens around the world
Long before she became an online celebrity, Jackie was believed to be the first documented bald eagle hatched in Big Bear Valley, according to Friends of Big Bear Valley.
Born in 2012, she emerged during a remarkable comeback for the bald eagle in California and throughout the United States. Decades earlier, the species had been pushed to the brink of extinction by habitat loss, hunting and the pesticide DDT. Conservation efforts helped restore populations, and Jackie became part of a new generation of nesting eagles in Southern California.
Her story unfolded in public view.
A wildlife camera installed near a nest high in a Jeffrey pine overlooking Big Bear Lake allowed viewers to watch every stage of her life, from nest-building and courtship to egg-laying and raising young.
What began as a conservation project grew into one of the most popular wildlife livestreams in the nation.
By 2026, Friends of Big Bear Valley had attracted more than a million followers across social media platforms, with viewers regularly tuning in from across California and around the world to watch Jackie and her mate, Shadow.
Jackie and Shadow's love story captured the world's attention
Jackie's popularity soared after she formed a pair bond with Shadow in 2018.
The pair became known for their devotion to one another and their resilience through years of triumph and heartbreak. Viewers watched them endure severe winter storms, failed nesting attempts, raven attacks and the loss of eggs and eaglets.
Yet they continued returning to the nest each season.
The pair successfully raised multiple offspring over the years, including Stormy and Spirit, and later Sunny and Gizmo, whose journeys drew worldwide attention. In 2026, Jackie and Shadow welcomed Luna and Sandy, the last eaglets she would raise before her illness.
For many viewers, Jackie represented something larger than a single eagle.
She became a symbol of perseverance, parenthood and the often-unpredictable realities of life in the wild.
A summer rescue that united eagle fans
Concern spread throughout the eagle-watching community during the summer of 2026 when Jackie disappeared from the nest area.
After days without sightings, she was found grounded near Big Bear Lake and transported to wildlife rehabilitation facilities before arriving at the Ojai Raptor Center.
Veterinarians diagnosed severe anemia, kidney inflammation and other complications. Despite intensive treatment and support from wildlife specialists, her condition remained critical.
Updates from her medical team were closely followed by thousands of supporters who flooded social media with messages of encouragement and prayers.
Her illness became a reminder that even the strongest animals face challenges unseen by those watching from afar.
Jackie becomes a TV celebrity
Jackie and Shadow were once featured on the CBS TV show "NCIS,” the episode is dubbed “Butterfly Effect” from Season 20, Episode 16.
The episode shows two agents with cell phones watching the Big Bear Bald Eagle Nest Cam, installed by the nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley.
The agents mention “Shadow” while watching a “bald eagle’s nest in the Yukon Territory” in northwest Canada despite the feed showing the nest in Big Bear.
The eagles are mentioned sporadically throughout the show as the NCIS team investigates who is responsible for a potential bio-terror attack at a strip mall parking garage.
Fascinated by Jackie and Shadow's love story, Apple Valley artist, bird-watcher and frequent visitor to Big Bear, Debbie Saude grabbed her paintbrushes and went to work.
Saude’s painting shows the eagle couple perched together on a tree branch high in the San Bernardino Mountains.
“Jackie and Shadow’s story is so bittersweet,” Saude told the Daily Press. “They’re so inspiring, mainly because they’ve been so dedicated to each other through the good and bad times.”
Jackie was more than a bird
Wildlife experts often remind the public not to humanize animals.
Yet Jackie made that difficult.
Teachers used her story in classrooms. Retirees and homebound viewers found companionship through the nest cameras. Families gathered around computers and televisions to watch her incubate eggs during snowstorms and feed hungry eaglets.
Throughout her life, many Californians learned about bald eagle conservation, nesting behavior, and the delicate ecosystems surrounding Big Bear Lake.
Her influence extended beyond wildlife education. Supporters frequently cited Jackie and Shadow when advocating for habitat preservation projects around the Big Bear area, including efforts to protect important eagle foraging grounds.
Jackie is survived by her longtime mate, Shadow, and multiple offspring that have dispersed into the wild over the years.
(This story was updated with new information.)

sources.news_title: Big Bear bald eagle Jackie dies after health "continued to deteriorate," California veterinary center says
sources.text:
Big Bear bald eagle Jackie dies after health "continued to deteriorate," California veterinary center says
Jackie, the bald eagle who gained national attention for raising eaglets in Big Bear with her partner Shadow, has died after receiving care in an animal care center, Ojai Raptor Center in California announced Monday.
The center, which cared for Jackie for her last three weeks, said she died in the early hours of Monday morning.
"It is with profound sadness that we share that [Jackie] passed away in the early hours of this morning, following more than three weeks of intensive medical care," the center said.
The veterinary center has detailed every step of Jackie's time in their care, including a series of setbacks that she faced due to anemia and a mystery illness that caused her packed cell volume to drop well below average. Despite undergoing a blood transfusion, Jackie's condition continued to worsen.
"Over the past several days, her condition continued to deteriorate despite intensive treatment and the combined efforts of our veterinary team and consulting specialists," Ojai Raptor Center said. "She remained critically ill, receiving oxygen therapy, supportive treatment, and around-the-clock monitoring in our intensive care unit."
Her remains have been transferred into the care of the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
Jackie had been in the care of the raptor center since July 17, when she was transferred following rescue by the Los Angeles County Department of Parks and Recreation's San Dimas Raptor Rescue team. They responded to the Dana Point Park area near Big Bear Lake after learning that she had been involved in a fight with two subadult eagles and was found to be "very sick."
Jackie and Shadow have gained national fame as their day-to-day lives have been observed for years via a livestream camera operated by the Friends of Big Bear Valley, a nonprofit wildlife organization.
Estimated by the Friends of Big Bear Valley to have lived about 14 years, Jackie mothered several eaglets to fledging with Shadow, including Simba, Spirit, Sunny, Gizmo and her two most recently hatched eaglets, Luna and Sandy.
The names were famously chosen by students at nearby Big Bear Elementary School. Sandy was named after the late Sandy Steers, the longtime FOBBV executive director who helped launch the livestream cameras. Steers died earlier this year.
In a statement, FOBBV urged the public to treat the organization and Ojai Raptor Center's staff with kindness in light of the news.
"Soar free Jackie," the organization said.

Beloved Bald Eagle Jackie Dies Weeks After Vicious Attack
Beloved California bald eagle Jackie is dead ... just weeks after suffering a brutal attack carried out by two other eagles ... ending weeks of hope that the iconic Big Bear bird would pull through.
The Ojai Raptor Center announced Monday that Jackie died early Monday morning after more than three weeks of intensive medical treatment.
The facility shared a remembrance photo of Jackie on Facebook, writing, "Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her."
Jackie had been fighting for her life since July, when she was attacked by two juvenile bald eagles. Folks across the country had been closely following updates on her condition as the raptor center worked around the clock to save her.
According to ORC, Jackie remained critically ill throughout her treatment, requiring oxygen therapy, supportive care and constant monitoring in the facility's intensive care unit. The center said Jackie's remains have now been transferred to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
ORC also thanked the countless people who rallied around Jackie during her fight, saying her story brought people together through their shared love of wildlife.
Jackie's death is especially heartbreaking for fans who had followed her for years as one half of a famous Big Bear bald eagle pair. Jackie and her longtime mate, Shadow, became beloved fixtures in the Southern California community and amassed a huge following through live cameras monitoring their nest at Big Bear Lake.
TMZ has closely followed Jackie's story, including her relationship with Shadow and the couple's nesting activity over the years. Their bond and efforts to raise eaglets turned them into something of a local celebrity couple ... with thousands of viewers tuning in to watch their lives unfold in real time.
Fans had been holding out hope Jackie would reunite with Shadow after surviving the attack ... but sadly, that reunion will never happen, and Shadow now remains an empty nester.
